overview.title: From statistical NLP to LSTMs and Transformers
overview.section: 14.1 A brief history of natural language processing
overview.main_topic: The rest of the NLP history: decision trees, then statistical models and learned parametric models; NLP as pattern recognition on words, with example tasks; the 2010s LSTM era and its limits; and the Transformer's scalability, which led to today's large language models.
overview.central_idea: Modern NLP is pattern recognition applied to words. It finds statistical regularities rather than human-like understanding, and that turns out to be enough for many tasks. LSTMs pushed accuracy up in the 2010s but struggled with long-range dependencies and slow training. The Transformer fixed the scalability problem: it keeps improving as model and data grow, and its training parallelises well.
overview.importance: It frames the three text chapters. It names the three canonical tasks (classification, translation, language modelling) that chapters 14-16 cover, explains why the book moves from LSTMs to Transformers, and sets a sober tone about what these models really do.
learning_objectives: Trace the progression decision trees → logistic regression → learned parametric models, and the declining role of hand-built linguistics.
Describe modern NLP as pattern recognition on text and give the page's three example tasks.
State the book's position that text models learn statistical regularities, not human-like understanding.
Explain the strengths and two limitations of LSTMs for NLP.
Explain why the Transformer scaled better: accuracy that improves with model and data size, and parallelisable training.
prerequisites: The early, rule-based history of NLP (p.406)
Logistic regression and the idea of parametric models (earlier chapters)

summary:
The page continues the history from p.406. The first ML approaches to NLP, based on decision trees, aimed to **automate the development of the if/then/else rules** of hardcoded systems. Then **statistical approaches** gained ground, **starting with logistic regression**. Over time **learned parametric models took over**, and some came to see linguistics baked directly into a model as a **hindrance**. Frederick Jelinek, an early speech-recognition researcher, joked: *"Every time I fire a linguist, the performance of the speech recognizer goes up."* (The book dates this to the 1990s; see the review flag.)

Just as **computer vision is pattern recognition applied to pixels**, **modern NLP is pattern recognition applied to words**. Three example applications:

- Spam probability of an email → **text classification**
- Most likely Russian translation of an English sentence → **translation**
- The next word of an incomplete sentence → **language modeling**

The models in this book **won't possess a human-like understanding of language**. They look for **statistical regularities**, which turns out to be enough for many real-world tasks.

In the last decade, researchers found how "shockingly effective" it can be to learn answers to **narrow statistical questions about text**. In the **2010s, LSTMs** were applied to text, greatly increasing parameter counts and compute. They generalised far better than earlier approaches but hit limits: they **struggled with dependencies across long text** (many sentences and paragraphs), and they were **slow and unwieldy to train** compared with vision models.

At the end of the 2010s, Google researchers found the **Transformer**, which solved many of these scalability issues. **If model size and training data grew together, Transformers kept getting more accurate**, and their training **could be parallelised effectively, even for long sequences**: doubling the machines roughly halves the wait. Together with faster GPUs and CPUs, this produced an explosion of investment. Chat systems such as **ChatGPT** captured public attention. Their training text is a significant portion of the internet's written language, and training one model can cost **tens of millions of dollars**. The page ends warning that some hype should be cut down to size: "these are pattern" (continued on p.408: "recognition machines").

paragraphs.excerpt: automate the development of the kind of if/then/else rules of hardcoded
paragraphs.what_it_says: Finishing p.406's sentence: the earliest ML approaches (decision trees) aimed to automate building the if/then/else rules of hardcoded systems. Then statistical approaches gained speed, starting with logistic regression. Over time, learned parametric models took over, and some came to see linguistics baked directly into a model as a hindrance. Jelinek joked, 'Every time I fire a linguist, the performance of the speech recognizer goes up.'
paragraphs.what_it_means: The field went from learned rules (trees), to learned weights over features (logistic regression), to models whose behaviour is almost entirely in learned parameters. Each step reduced the hand-engineered linguistic knowledge in the system. Jelinek's joke sums up the empirical finding that, given enough data, letting the model learn often beats encoding expert assumptions by hand.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It explains why this book's text chapters skip hand-crafted linguistic features (p.408) and go straight to learned models. It also continues the book's general theme that learned representations beat engineered ones when there is enough data.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Logistic regression on text models $P(y=1\mid x)=\sigma(w^\top x+b)$, where $x$ is a feature vector such as word counts. This is exactly the kind of bag-of-words model built in section 14.4, in neural form: a `Dense(1, activation="sigmoid")` layer on multi-hot inputs. (Beyond the book on this page.)

A model whose behaviour is set by a fixed set of learned parameters (weights).

paragraphs.what_it_says: Just as computer vision is pattern recognition on pixels, modern NLP is pattern recognition on words, with many practical applications. The bullets that follow (p407_e05 to p407_e09) give three: the probability that an email is spam (text classification), the most likely Russian translation of an English sentence (translation), and the likely next word of an incomplete sentence (language modeling).
paragraphs.what_it_means: The same deep learning machinery from the vision chapters applies to text once text is encoded as tensors. The three tasks map onto the book's next chapters: classification (chapter 14), translation and language modelling (chapter 15), and generation built on language models (chapter 16).
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It gives the reader a map of task types and shows that the methods transfer across modalities.
paragraphs.technical_idea: The three tasks differ in output structure. Classification gives one label per text. Translation gives a sequence conditioned on a sequence. Language modelling gives a distribution over the next token, $P(w_t\mid w_{<t})$. (Beyond the book.)

terminology.meaning: Assigning a category or probability to a text, e.g. spam versus not spam.
Mapping a sentence in one language to its most likely equivalent in another.
Predicting the next word (token) given the preceding ones.

paragraphs.excerpt: The text-processing models you will train in this book won’t possess
paragraphs.what_it_says: The text models in this book won't have a human-like understanding of language. They look for statistical regularities in their input, which turns out to be enough to perform well on many real-world tasks.
paragraphs.what_it_means: A sentiment classifier that learns 'terrible' predicts a negative review doesn't know what a film is or why people dislike things. It has learned correlations between token patterns and labels. The surprising result is how far such correlations go.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It sets realistic expectations and protects against over-attributing intelligence to models, a point the page returns to with ChatGPT and continues on p.408.

terminology.meaning: Patterns of co-occurrence and correlation in data that a model can exploit to predict outputs.

connections: p.408: 'these are pattern recognition machines' that copy and synthesise training data, unlike human intelligence

paragraphs.excerpt: In the last decade, NLP researchers and practitioners have discovered just
paragraphs.what_it_says: In the last decade, NLP researchers found how shockingly effective it is to learn answers to narrow statistical questions about text. In the 2010s, LSTMs were applied to text, greatly increasing parameter counts and compute requirements. LSTMs generalised to unseen examples far more accurately than earlier approaches, but hit limits: they struggled to track dependencies across long chains of text with many sentences and paragraphs, and compared with vision models they were slow and unwieldy to train.
paragraphs.what_it_means: LSTMs (chapter 13) were a big step up but have two structural weaknesses. (1) All context has to squeeze through a fixed-size state passed step by step, so information from far back fades. (2) Each step depends on the previous one, so computation over the sequence can't be parallelised across timesteps.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: These limits motivate the Transformer in the next paragraph and in chapter 15. They also explain why the LSTM-based classifiers in this chapter are a stepping stone rather than the endpoint.
paragraphs.technical_idea: The sequential bottleneck: computing $h_t=f(h_{t-1},x_t)$ requires $h_{t-1}$, so a length-$T$ sequence needs $T$ dependent steps. Convolutional vision models have no such chain and parallelise well on GPUs. (Beyond the book.)

terminology.meaning: A relationship between tokens far apart in a text, e.g. a pronoun and its referent several sentences earlier.
Specific prediction tasks, such as 'which word comes next?', learned from data.

connections: p.393: the LSTM layer introduced in chapter 13
p.461: chapter 15 notes RNNs progressively forget the past and struggle with very long sequences

paragraphs.excerpt: Toward the end of the 2010s, researchers at Google discovered a
paragraphs.what_it_says: Toward the end of the 2010s, Google researchers found a new architecture, the Transformer, that solved many of the LSTMs' scalability issues. As long as model size and training data increased together, Transformers seemed to keep getting more accurate. Their training computations could also be parallelised effectively, even for long sequences: doubling the training machines roughly halves the wait for a result.
paragraphs.what_it_means: There are two separate advantages. (1) Scaling behaviour: accuracy keeps improving as you grow model and data together instead of plateauing. (2) Parallelism: there is no step-by-step recurrence, so all positions can be processed at once and training spreads efficiently across hardware.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: These properties made very large language models practical. They are why the book spends chapter 15 on the Transformer.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: the paper is Vaswani et al., 2017, 'Attention Is All You Need', cited on p.461. The 'grow model and data together' observation was later formalised as neural scaling laws. 'Halve the time by doubling machines' is the ideal of near-linear data-parallel scaling, which real systems only approximate.

terminology.meaning: An attention-based architecture without recurrence, introduced by Google researchers in 2017.
Splitting the training computation across many devices so they work at the same time.

paragraphs.what_it_says: The Transformer, together with ever-faster GPUs and CPUs, led to an explosion of investment and interest in NLP over the past few years. Chat systems like ChatGPT captured public attention with fluent text on seemingly arbitrary topics. Their training text is a significant portion of all written language on the internet, and training a single model can cost tens of millions of dollars. Some hype should be cut down to size: these are pattern (recognition machines, p.408).
paragraphs.what_it_means: Today's large language models come from a scalable architecture combined with very large data and compute. The authors credit the impressive results but immediately call these models pattern recognisers. That ties back to the earlier paragraph's point about statistical regularities rather than understanding.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It puts the book's material in the current landscape and gives a balanced view: an impressive empirical result, but not human intelligence.

concepts.name: Statistical / learned NLP
concepts.definition: NLP based on models that learn parameters from data (starting with logistic regression) instead of hand-written rules.
concepts.intuition: Let the data decide which words and patterns matter.
concepts.technical: Progression on the page: decision trees → logistic regression → learned parametric models, with hand-built linguistics increasingly seen as a hindrance.
concepts.significance: The basis for all the models in chapters 14-16.
concepts.example: A logistic regression over word counts for spam detection.
concepts.misconception: That linguistic knowledge is always needed for good NLP performance. Jelinek's joke suggests otherwise, at least with enough data.

concepts.name: Language modeling
concepts.definition: Predicting which word will likely come next given an incomplete sentence.
concepts.technical: Learn $P(w_t\mid w_1,\dots,w_{t-1})$ from large text corpora. Simple 'guess the missing word' training underlies chat systems (p.408).
concepts.significance: The training setup behind modern large language models such as ChatGPT. Covered in chapter 15.
concepts.misconception: That predicting the next word requires or implies human-like understanding.

concepts.name: LSTM for text (and its limits)
concepts.definition: Recurrent networks with gated memory, applied to text in the 2010s.
concepts.intuition: Read a document word by word with a notepad that can be selectively updated.
concepts.technical: More accurate than earlier approaches, but they struggle with dependencies across many sentences or paragraphs and are slow and unwieldy to train, because each step depends on the previous one.
concepts.significance: Dominant in 2010s NLP. Replaced by Transformers.
concepts.example: Bidirectional LSTMs were state of the art on many NLP tasks around 2016 (p.402).
concepts.misconception: That LSTMs were abandoned because they didn't work. They worked well but didn't scale.

concepts.name: Transformer
concepts.definition: An architecture introduced by Google researchers at the end of the 2010s that solved many LSTM scalability problems.
concepts.intuition: Instead of passing a note down a line of people, everyone in the room can look at everyone else at once.
concepts.technical: Accuracy kept improving as model size and data grew together, and training parallelised well even for long sequences.
concepts.significance: The basis of today's large language models and chat systems.
concepts.example: ChatGPT-style systems trained on a significant fraction of internet text.
concepts.misconception: That the Transformer understands language like a human. The authors call these models pattern-recognition machines.

concepts.name: NLP as pattern recognition
concepts.definition: Modern NLP is pattern recognition applied to words, as computer vision is pattern recognition applied to pixels.
concepts.intuition: Find which word patterns predict which outputs.
concepts.technical: Models capture statistical regularities, not human-like understanding.
concepts.significance: Frames what the book's text models can and can't do.
concepts.example: Spam classification by detecting suspicious word patterns.

deeper.title: Why recurrence is hard to parallelise and attention isn't
deeper.body:
1. An LSTM computes $h_1$ from $x_1$, then $h_2$ from $h_1$ and $x_2$, and so on: $T$ steps that must run in order.
2. A GPU can't start step $t$ before step $t-1$ finishes, so a long document means a long chain of small computations.
3. Information from step 1 must survive $T-1$ state updates to influence step $T$, which explains the trouble with long-range dependencies.
4. A Transformer computes interactions between all pairs of positions with matrix multiplications, all at once. There's no chain, so the work fills the GPU and spreads across machines.

The page states the outcome (LSTMs slow and limited on long text; Transformers parallelisable and scalable). This mechanism-level explanation is added here and is developed in chapter 15.

deeper.title: Firing linguists
deeper.body: Jelinek's joke is like a chef who discovers that their dish improves every time they stop following an old recipe book and instead taste-test with thousands of diners. The recipe book (linguistic rules) encodes real knowledge, but where it is rigid or wrong it gets in the way of what the feedback (data) shows.

misconceptions.claim: The text models in this book understand language like humans do.
misconceptions.correction: The authors state they won't have human-like understanding. They exploit statistical regularities, which is enough for many tasks.
They generalised far better than previous approaches. Their limits were long-range dependencies and slow, unwieldy training.

misconceptions.claim: The Transformer's advantage is only accuracy.
misconceptions.correction: The page stresses scalability: accuracy kept improving as model and data grew, and training could be parallelised even for long sequences.

misconceptions.claim: Doubling machines always exactly halves training time.
misconceptions.correction: The page says 'roughly'. In practice, communication overhead makes scaling sub-linear (beyond the book).

takeaways: NLP went from decision trees to logistic regression to learned parametric models, with hand-built linguistics increasingly seen as a hindrance.
Modern NLP is pattern recognition applied to words. Example tasks: text classification, translation, language modeling.
These models learn statistical regularities, not human-like understanding.
2010s LSTMs were more accurate but struggled with long-range dependencies and were slow to train.
The Transformer scaled: it improved as model and data grew and trained in parallel. That made ChatGPT-scale models possible, at tens of millions of dollars per model.

questions.question: Which two limitations of LSTMs for NLP does the page name?
options: They couldn't generalise to unseen examples and needed hand-written rules
They struggled with dependencies across long text and were slow and unwieldy to train
They had too few parameters and required linguistic features
They couldn't be used for classification and couldn't be stacked
questions.answer: They struggled with dependencies across long text and were slow and unwieldy to train
questions.explanation: The page says LSTMs generalised far better than previous approaches (so the first option is wrong) but struggled with long chains of text and were slow to train compared with vision models. The page says LSTMs dramatically *increased* parameter counts, and nothing on it suggests they couldn't classify or be stacked.

questions.question: Match each example application on the page with its task name.
questions.answer: Email spam probability → text classification; most likely Russian translation of an English sentence → translation; the next word of an incomplete sentence → language modeling.
questions.explanation: These are the three bullets on the page.

questions.question: What two properties of the Transformer does the page credit for solving the LSTMs' scalability issues?
questions.answer: (1) Its accuracy kept improving as model size and training data increased together. (2) Its training could be parallelised effectively even for long sequences, so doubling the machines roughly halves training time.
questions.explanation: Both are stated in the 'Toward the end of the 2010s' paragraph.

questions.question: What does Jelinek's joke 'Every time I fire a linguist, the performance of the speech recognizer goes up' illustrate?
questions.answer: That hand-built linguistic knowledge baked into a model came to be seen as a hindrance, and that learned parametric models trained on data often outperformed systems with hand-engineered linguistic rules.
questions.explanation: The page uses the quote to illustrate learned models taking over from embedded linguistics.

questions.question: What is the authors' position on whether the book's text models understand language?
options: They have human-like understanding once trained on enough data
They don't understand language; they find statistical regularities, which is enough for many tasks
They understand syntax but not meaning
They can't perform well on real-world tasks
questions.answer: They don't understand language; they find statistical regularities, which is enough for many tasks
questions.explanation: That's stated directly. The first option contradicts the page. The third option's syntax/semantics split isn't the authors' claim. The fourth contradicts 'sufficient to perform well on a wide array of real-world tasks'.

questions.question: Why does the page draw an analogy between computer vision and NLP?
questions.answer: Both are pattern recognition, one on pixels and one on words. That suggests the same deep learning toolkit applies to text once it is turned into numeric tensors, which is the topic of section 14.2.
questions.explanation: The page says 'Much as computer vision is pattern recognition applied to pixels, the modern field of NLP is all about pattern recognition applied to words in text.'

questions.question: Using what you learned about RNNs in chapter 13, can you explain in your own words why an LSTM is hard to parallelise across timesteps?
questions.answer: Each hidden state depends on the previous one ($h_t = f(h_{t-1}, x_t)$), so timesteps must be processed in order. You can't compute step 100 before step 99.
questions.explanation: This connects the page's claim that LSTMs were slow to train with the recurrence mechanism from chapter 13 (p.390). The page itself doesn't give the mechanism.
